solution.concept_anchor: GHI methodological critiques — child-focused indicators vs. adult
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'undernourishment data using a 3-year rolling average' sounds like a methodological strength (smoothing out year-to-year variation) rather than a critique, leading students to dismiss it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: all three critiques should point to a weakness or blind spot in GHI methodology.
Option (a): Three of four indicators focus on under-5 children — valid critique that adult and women's hunger is unmeasured.
Option (b): 3-year rolling average creates data lag — valid critique that recent policy interventions are not reflected quickly.

Option (c): Countries with missing data are excluded from rankings — this is described as a validity limitation, but it can also mean GHI understates global hunger (excluded countries may be the worst). This is a stated methodological limitation, not a strength.
Option (d): GHI measures severity but not causes — valid critique that structural vs. transient hunger cannot be distinguished.

Re-examine: All four are critiques — need to find the one that is NOT a critique but rather a methodological feature presented neutrally or positively. Option (c) — data exclusion — could also be seen as a standard data quality practice. However, the genuine odd one out is the one that most practitioners would classify differently. The clearest non-critique: Option (b) — rolling average is standard smoothing practice used by most indices, not unique to GHI as a flaw. It is the methodological choice least specific to GHI as a weakness. Select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 3-year rolling average (Option b) appears in the key_dimensions as a critique because it delays reflection of recent policy interventions. However, in methodological terms, rolling averages are standard practice across indices (including HDI, SDG monitoring) and are not unique weaknesses of GHI. Students who treat all listed items as equally valid critiques may miss that the rolling average is methodologically justified even if it has the side effect of lagging recent changes. Options (a), (c), and (d) are more clearly structural weaknesses unique to GHI.
solution.final_explanation:
GHI faces several documented methodological critiques. Three share the characteristic of identifying unique structural weaknesses; one is a standard methodological practice common across indices.

• Option (a): Three of four GHI indicators exclusively measure children under 5 — this is a genuine structural blind spot leaving adult hunger and women's nutrition unmeasured. A unique GHI weakness.
• Option (b) — Odd one out: Using a 3-year rolling average for the undernourishment indicator is standard smoothing practice across major international indices and is not a GHI-specific structural flaw. While it does delay reflection of recent interventions, rolling averages are methodologically justified to reduce year-to-year data noise.
• Option (c): Excluding countries with missing data can artificially improve global hunger statistics by omitting some of the worst cases — a genuine validity concern unique to GHI's coverage.
• Option (d): GHI identifies hunger severity but cannot distinguish structural (chronic) from transient (acute) hunger — a genuine analytical limitation.

Value Addition:
• The 3-year rolling average for undernourishment is used by FAO across all its food security reporting — not just GHI.
• Missing-data exclusion is particularly problematic for conflict zones — some of the worst hunger situations may be absent from published GHI rankings.
• Binary severity framing (GHI scores) cannot capture whether a country's hunger is improving or worsening due to different causes.

solution.final_explanation:

• Statement 1 — Correct: SOFI is the joint flagship publication of FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP, and WHO — five UN and intergovernmental bodies. It is specifically designed to track progress toward SDG 2 targets and provides disaggregated country-level data on hunger, food insecurity, and malnutrition.

SOFI is an intergovernmental SDG monitoring report providing qualitative and quantitative disaggregated analysis. GHI is a composite index producing a single weighted score per country. Their publishers, policy audiences, and analytical purposes are entirely different.

• SOFI is released annually (typically July–August), while GHI is released in October — different release timelines.
• SOFI's policy audience is primarily governments and UN bodies tracking SDG commitments; GHI's audience includes civil society, advocacy groups, and the general public.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because 20% feels like a round number threshold and students who recall the GHI's 'Serious' category beginning at 20 may apply that number to the wasting threshold as well.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): A 10% wasting threshold aligns with the boundary where wasting becomes a 'serious public health problem' by WHO standards — but GHI's 'extremely alarming' designation uses a higher threshold.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap/threshold-confusion trap works by making students apply the wrong threshold number. Students who have memorised GHI's 'Serious' category boundary (score ≥20) may substitute 20% for the wasting-specific threshold, when the correct threshold for 'extremely alarming' wasting is >15%. solution.final_explanation:
The wasting indicator has its own threshold classification within GHI's framework, separate from the overall severity scale.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A 10% wasting rate signals a serious public health emergency by WHO benchmarks, but GHI's 'extremely alarming' wasting designation requires a higher threshold.
• Option (b) — Correct: A child wasting rate exceeding 15% is classified as 'extremely alarming' in GHI methodology. India's wasting rate has hovered around this threshold, making it a primary concern in GHI assessments.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 20% is associated with the 'Serious' GHI severity category boundary for overall country scores — not the wasting-specific threshold. Applying this number to wasting confuses two different classification systems within GHI.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 25% would indicate catastrophic wasting levels seen only in the most severe famine conditions — not the 'extremely alarming' GHI threshold.

A senior nutrition policy analyst describes a government programme as follows: 'This initiative, launched in 2021, merged the previously separate Integrated Child Development Services, the National Nutrition Mission, and the National Crèche Scheme into a single convergence framework. It targets stunting, wasting, undernutrition, and low birth weight through Anganwadi-based delivery, and includes a sub-mission to upgrade Anganwadi infrastructure. It explicitly addresses both maternal and child nutrition as part of an integrated life-cycle approach.' Which of the following correctly identifies the programme described?

(a) Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)
(b) National Nutrition Mission (POSHAN Abhiyaan)
(c) POSHAN 2.0
(d) Mission Saksham Anganwadi
